summary:
The HEARTS Act of 2024 (Pub. L. 118-176, enacted December 23, 2024, originating as H.R. 6829) amends the Public Health Service Act (PHSA) by inserting four new sections—312A through 312D (codified at 42 U.S.C. 244a–244d)—immediately after PHSA § 312 (42 U.S.C. 244). Its purpose is to direct the development and dissemination of cardiomyopathy education, awareness, and risk-assessment materials; authorize related research and surveillance; and authorize a grant program for AED and CPR access in schools. Notably, § 2(b) provides that no additional funds are authorized to be appropriated to carry out any of the four new sections, so the operative mandates must be executed within existing appropriations.

New PHSA § 312A directs the Secretary, in consultation with the CDC Director, to develop public education materials—covering signs, symptoms, and risk factors of specified high-risk cardiac conditions (including cardiomyopathy and enumerated genetic arrhythmia syndromes), AED placement guidelines, AED/CPR training information, and cardiac emergency response plan recommendations—not later than 18 months after enactment, and to disseminate them (via State educational agencies, health departments/professionals, and CDC website posting) not later than 30 months after enactment. Subsection (c) supplies definitions, incorporating ESEA § 8101 terms.

New PHSA § 312B requires the Secretary, acting through the CDC Director, to submit to Congress within 18 months a report on existing CDC activities concerning cardiomyopathy prevalence and epidemiology (including natural history and estimates of emergency department visits and hospitalizations), to be made public subject to applicable federal and state privacy laws. Subsection (b) directs development of a publicly available cardiomyopathy risk assessment for providers and individuals—including background information, risk and progression worksheets, and screening guidelines—developed with input from patient advocacy organizations, medical professional societies, and relevant federal agencies.

New PHSA § 312C provides discretionary authority (the Secretary "may," in consultation with the NIH Director) to expand and coordinate NIH research on cardiomyopathy causation, long-term outcomes, and longitudinal/retrospective treatment studies, subject to a nonduplication requirement, and mandates an NIH report to Congress within 18 months outlining ongoing efforts and a research agenda.

New PHSA § 312D authorizes the Secretary to award grants (discretionary) to eligible entities—local educational agencies (including qualifying public charter schools), in consultation with a qualified health care entity—to promote student access to AEDs and CPR in public schools. Permissible uses include program materials, training, cardiac emergency response plans, and purchase/maintenance of AEDs approved, cleared, or classified under FDCA §§ 515, 510(k), or 513(f)(2). The section defines "qualified health care entity" (a public or 501(c)/501(a) tax-exempt entity meeting capacity criteria) and incorporates ESEA § 8101 definitions.
